title: Lament: A Bible Study on Praying Your Pain
subtitle: A five-session study on suffering and lament, anchored in the Psalms and Job.
summary:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who have sat in a church that knew how to praise and did not know what to do with a person who could not. It walks slowly through five movements on suffering and the lost prayer the church forgot how to pray. It begins with lament as a vanished form, the cost of a worship that only ascends and never cries out. It moves into the lament psalms themselves, the how long of Psalm 13 and the unbroken dark of Psalm 88, the one prayer in the book that does not resolve. It sits with Job and the friends who explained too much, the failure of the tidy answer, the long silence in the ash. It comes to the cross, where God does not stand above the sufferer offering an explanation but climbs down inside the suffering and cries the lament himself. And it ends not in resolution but in a hope that refuses to be denial, the difference between an answer and a presence, between the question closed and the question carried.

This is not a study that will hurry anyone out of their grief. It will not hand a suffering person the platitude that everything happens for a reason, and the leader must never let it. Walter Brueggemann taught the church the cost of what he called the loss of lament, the price a community pays when it permits only praise. The Psalms gave Israel a language for the dark that the modern church has largely thrown away, and Job stands as the long protest God did not rebuke. The study holds the honesty of Psalm 88 without flinching. That psalm ends in darkness, and that is allowed. Most of all it implicates the leader and the writer. James Bell does not stand outside this. He was raised without a father, and he came to God out of atheism, and he has prayed prayers that got no answer he could see. He has stood at gravesides and had nothing to say that did not sound like a lie. He writes from inside the loss. So will you.
audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

sessions.title: The Language the Church Forgot
sessions.aim: To name lament as a lost form of prayer, neither rebellion against God nor a failure of faith, and to count the cost of a worship that has learned only to praise and forgotten how to cry out.
sessions.summary: A man told Bell, after a funeral, that he had stopped coming to church because there was no room in it for how he actually felt. He was not angry at God. He was grieving, and every song the church sang told him to be grateful, and he had nothing left to be grateful with. He was not faithless. He had simply been handed a worship that ran in one direction only, upward, and his grief had nowhere to go. The first question is not how to feel better. It is why the church forgot how to pray the way half the Psalms pray. Bell takes the strong form of two instincts that want to silence each other. The first says that faith praises, that a Christian gives thanks in all circumstances, that complaint is the opposite of trust, and it is right that Scripture commands gratitude and that grumbling against God can be a real sin. The second says that honesty demands the freedom to rage, that suppressing grief is a lie, and it is right that buried pain festers and that a faith that cannot tell the truth is not worth much. Bell will not let either win cleanly. Praise is not the only faithful prayer, which refutes the first, and lament is not mere venting, which refutes the second. Lament is a form, an ancient and disciplined form, a complaint addressed to God and not away from him, a protest that is itself an act of faith because you do not bother to argue with a God you have abandoned. The church did not lose lament because it grew more faithful. It lost it because it grew more comfortable. And the cost is a generation of believers who think their grief disqualifies them from the room.

keyScripture.why: How long, O Lord. Will you forget me forever. The psalmist opens not with praise but with a complaint flung straight at God, and Scripture preserves it as prayer, naming the cry of the forgotten as a faithful address and not a failure of belief.

discussion.q: Before tonight, did you believe a faithful Christian was allowed to complain to God, or did you carry the sense that real faith only ever gives thanks?
discussion.behind: Surface the default before defining anything. Most people in the room have an unexamined rule that complaint equals weak faith, and they have been quietly ashamed of their own grief because of it. The point is not to settle the question yet but to expose the rule and the shame attached to it. Land it on honesty, not consensus. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Roughly a third of the Psalms are laments, prayers of complaint, and most of us could not name one. Why do you think the church sings the praise psalms constantly and almost never the laments?
discussion.behind: Move the room to notice the absence. We did not decide to drop lament on theological grounds, we simply stopped finding it useful in a worship built for comfort. Help them feel that the omission is not neutral, that a whole half of biblical prayer has gone missing from our mouths, and ask what that does to a grieving person.

discussion.q: Bell says the church lost lament not because it grew more faithful but because it grew more comfortable. Where have you felt the pressure to perform gratitude you did not feel, to sing along when you were falling apart?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge of the session. Do not let it become a debate about whether complaint is allowed in theory. Keep it on the personal recognition that we have all, including the leader, faked a praise we did not have because the room left no other option. The honesty here protects everyone who comes after.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong form of the view that faith always praises, that Scripture commands thanksgiving. What is true in that, and what does it become when it forgets the grieving person sitting in the pew?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness from the start. Scripture does command gratitude, and grumbling against God can be a real refusal of trust. Make sure the room does not leave thinking complaint is always righteous. The error is not the call to praise. It is the call to praise swung as a rule at a person who is in the dark.

discussion.q: Bell confesses he has stood at gravesides with nothing true to say and reached for a comfortable line anyway. Where have you handed a suffering person a tidy answer because the silence felt unbearable?
discussion.behind: Move from diagnosis to self-implication. You are not hunting for confession to shame anyone. You want each person, the leader first, inside the failure, because we have all reached for the platitude rather than sit in the dark with someone. Go first.

objections.objection: Complaining to God is just unbelief dressed up in spiritual language. Scripture says give thanks in all circumstances, and if you were really trusting God you would praise him through the pain, not argue with him about it.
objections.response: Sit with the half that is true, because Bell grants it. Scripture does command thanksgiving, and there is a grumbling against God, the kind Israel did in the wilderness, that is a real refusal to trust him. Then make the distinction with care. The same book that commands gratitude gives us Psalm 13 and Psalm 88 and the whole long protest of Job, and God does not rebuke any of it. Lament is not unbelief. It is the opposite. You do not bother to argue with a God you have given up on. The complaint is addressed to God, it stays in the relationship, it assumes he is there and ought to act, which is why the psalmist asks how long rather than walking away in silence. To tell a grieving person that their cry is faithlessness is not faith. It is cruelty, and it drives the brokenhearted out of the one room where they might have been met.

objections.objection: Lament is just venting, emotional release with a religious label on it. Sitting around complaining about your pain does not help anyone. You should pray for strength and move on, not wallow in the grief.
objections.response: Grant what is right, because some of it is. Pain that only circles itself, that rehearses the wound endlessly with no direction, can become a pit, and the church is right to want people to find their feet again. Then press the other edge gently. Lament is not venting, because venting is aimed at no one and asks for nothing. Lament is a form, disciplined and addressed, a complaint brought to God with a request attached and very often a turn toward trust at the end. It is not wallowing. It is the soul refusing to lie about its condition while still holding on to the One who could change it. To collapse lament into venting is to miss that the Psalms are prayer, structured prayer, the slow honest work of bringing the worst of what is true to the only One who can finally do anything about it.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the grief you have never brought to God in plain words, the one you have only ever prayed around because you were afraid the complaint itself was a sin?
sessions.practice: This week, write one honest lament of your own, on paper, addressed to God. Do not clean it up. Name the thing that hurts, say plainly what you wish he would do, and ask him your real question, even the how long, even the why. Do not force a happy ending onto it. If a turn toward trust comes, let it come, and if it does not come this week, leave it open. Bring the page to nothing but God.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we were taught to praise you and we were never taught to cry out to you, and so we have carried our grief alone, in silence, ashamed of the very tears you gave us. Forgive the church for the room it did not make. Forgive us for the times we handed a hurting person a tidy answer because we could not bear to sit in the dark with them. Teach us the prayer we forgot, the honest cry that stays in the room with you. You who kept Psalm 13 and Psalm 88 in your book, give us back the language of lament. Amen.
reflection: Where have I believed that my grief disqualifies me from worship, when a third of the Psalms are grief brought straight to God?
Have I ever shamed myself, or let someone shame me, for a complaint to God that Scripture would have called prayer?
If the church I sit in only ever sings upward, what has happened to the part of me that needed to cry out, and where has it gone?
sessions.teaching: Start where Bell starts, with a man after a funeral. He told Bell he had stopped coming to church because there was no room in it for how he actually felt. He was not angry at God, he said. He was grieving, and every song the church put in his mouth told him to be grateful, and he had run clean out of gratitude. He was not a faithless man. He had simply been handed a worship that ran in one direction only, upward, all ascent and no descent, and his grief had found no place to land. So we begin not with how to feel better, which is where everyone wants to begin, but with a harder and stranger question. Why did the church forget how to pray the way half its own prayer book prays. Take the two instincts that want to silence each other, and take them at their strongest. The first says faith praises. It points to the plain commands of Scripture, give thanks in all circumstances, rejoice always, and it concludes that complaint is the opposite of trust, that a grumbling Christian is a small one. And it is not entirely wrong. Scripture does command gratitude. There is a grumbling against God, the kind Israel did in the desert with the manna falling around them, that is a genuine refusal to trust, and pretending otherwise would be its own lie. The second instinct says honesty demands the freedom to rage, that to bury grief is to lie, that a faith which cannot tell the truth about pain is worthless. And this is not wrong either. Buried pain festers. A worship that requires you to fake a peace you do not have will eventually drive out everyone who is actually suffering, which is, sooner or later, everyone. Now watch what happens when you refuse to let either instinct take the whole field. Praise is not the only faithful prayer, which destroys the first position, because if it were, then a third of the Psalms, the inspired prayer book of the people of God, would be a record of faithlessness, which is absurd. The Spirit did not preserve Psalm 13 and Psalm 88 as examples of what not to do. He gave them to us as prayer. But lament is also not mere venting, which destroys the second position, because venting is aimed at no one and asks for nothing, while lament is a form, an ancient and disciplined form, and it is addressed. This is the whole thing, and the leader must hold it cleanly. Lament is a complaint addressed to God and not away from him. It is protest that stays in the room. And that is precisely why it is an act of faith and not its abandonment, because you do not bother to argue with a God you have walked away from. The psalmist cries how long, O Lord, will you forget me forever, and every word of it assumes God is there, that he ought to be acting, that the relationship is real enough to fight inside of. The man who shouts at heaven still believes someone is home. So here is the verdict, and it should unsettle us. The church did not lose lament because it became more faithful. It lost it because it became more comfortable. Walter Brueggemann named this decades ago, the costly loss of lament, and the cost is exactly what that man at the funeral was describing. When a worshiping community permits only praise, it tells its suffering members that their grief has no place at the table, that to belong they must perform a gratitude they do not feel, and so the grieving go quiet, or they go home. And I have to stand inside this failure, because I have committed it. I have stood at the edge of a grave with a family I love and felt the silence press in, and reached, God forgive me, for a comfortable line, a reason, a tidy verse, because I could not bear to let the silence be the silence. I gave an answer when I should have given my presence and my tears. The law names the writer before the reader. So we begin by recovering something we threw away. Not the abandonment of praise, never that, the Psalms climb to praise as surely as they descend into the dark. But the recovery of the other half, the descent, the cry, the how long. Because a faith that can only sing on the mountain has nothing to say in the valley, and the valley is where most of a life is lived, and it is where, as we will see, God himself finally came.

scriptureStudy.note: How long, O Lord. Will you forget me forever. The psalm opens with four how longs in two verses, a complaint hurled directly at God. Notice it is addressed to him, not about him. The protest stays inside the relationship, which is what makes it prayer and not abandonment.

I am the man who has seen affliction. The poet says God has walled him in so his prayer cannot get out, an astonishing accusation kept in Scripture. The book is literally named for lament, an entire book of the Bible given over to grief that does not pretend.

Job opened his mouth and cursed the day of his birth. The sufferer wishes he had never been born, and God does not strike him down for it. The honesty of grief is given room here that our worship rarely allows.

I am weary with my moaning, every night I flood my bed with tears. The psalmist describes exhaustion and weeping without apology, and the Spirit preserved it as a model of prayer, not a confession of weakness.

Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. Jesus pronounces a blessing on the grieving, not on those who have hurried past their grief. Mourning is named as a condition God meets, not a failure he tolerates.

Weep with those who weep. Paul commands the church to enter the grief of its members, not to argue them out of it. The body is to make room for the cry, which is the very room the church so often refuses.

O Lord, God of my salvation, I cry out day and night before you. Even the darkest psalm begins by addressing God as the God of salvation. The complaint that follows is unrelenting, but it is aimed at the One the psalmist still calls his God.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the history of what the church did with its own prayer book, because the loss of lament has a shape worth seeing. Walter Brueggemann, in his essay on the costly loss of lament and in The Message of the Psalms, traced how the worshiping community gradually edited the laments out of its functional life, keeping them in the canon but dropping them from the lectionary, the hymnal, and the mouth. The praise psalms stayed, the grief psalms went quiet, and the loss was not a neutral act of liturgical housekeeping. Brueggemann argued it cost the community two things. It cost them honesty, the capacity to bring the real condition of a life to God, and it cost them a certain kind of justice, because lament is also the form in which the oppressed name what is wrong and call God to act, so a church that cannot lament becomes a church that cannot protest. Set this against the wider story of worship in the modern West, where the market for praise music rewards the upbeat and the resolved and has almost no category for the song that ends in the dark. A serious group should weigh both edges. Consider what is gained by a worship oriented toward praise, the genuine lifting of the eyes to God, the refusal to be ruled by circumstance. Then weigh what is lost when praise becomes the only permitted note, when a grieving widow is handed a chorus about victory and told to sing it. The discipline this study asks is to recover the full range of biblical prayer, to let the room sing both the ascent and the descent, so that the praise, when it comes, is the praise of people who have been allowed to tell the truth first.

memoryVerse.text: How long, O Lord. Will you forget me forever. How long will you hide your face from me.

sessions.title: How Long, O Lord
sessions.aim: To learn the form of the lament psalm, to see how it addresses God with the complaint rather than around it, and to sit honestly with both Psalm 13, which turns, and Psalm 88, which does not.
sessions.summary: The lament psalms have a shape, and learning the shape gives the grieving a path to walk. Most of them move through the same movements, an address to God, a complaint laid out plainly, a petition that asks for something specific, and very often a turn, a vow of trust or a note of praise at the end. Psalm 13 is the clearest example. It opens with how long four times in two verses, names the enemy and the sorrow, asks God to consider and answer, and then turns, but I have trusted in your steadfast love. The first question is what to make of that turn, whether it is the goal of every lament, the happy ending we are all supposed to reach. Bell takes the strong form of the instinct that says yes, that the turn is the point, that a lament is only complete when it resolves into trust. He grants the weight of it. Psalm 13 does turn, and the turn is real and beautiful. But then he sets Psalm 88 beside it, and Psalm 88 does not turn. It is the one lament in the whole book that ends in the dark, its last word, in the Hebrew, is darkness. There is no resolution, no vow of praise, no but. The psalmist says God has put his companions far from him and the darkness is his only friend, and then the psalm simply stops. The turn, it cries out. Then the verdict that this session is built to protect. Psalm 88 is in the Bible too. God kept it. Which means a prayer that ends in the dark is still a prayer, that you are allowed to cry out and not feel better, that the lament which never resolves is not a failed lament but a faithful one. Some nights the turn does not come, and Scripture itself sits with you in that night and does not rush you out of it.

keyScripture.why: You have caused my beloved and my friend to shun me, my companions have become darkness. The darkest psalm in the book ends here, with no turn, no resolution, the final word in the Hebrew being darkness itself, and God preserved it as prayer, making room in Scripture for the grief that does not yet feel better.

discussion.q: Psalm 13 opens with how long asked four times in two verses. What does it do to you to hear the Bible itself ask God how long, and to keep asking it?
discussion.behind: Open on the gut response to the bluntness. Many have never noticed that Scripture talks to God this way, and the recognition can be a relief or a shock. The aim is to let the room feel that the impatient, repeated cry is not a lapse but a form, that the how long is sanctioned, so they stop policing it in themselves.

discussion.q: The lament psalms tend to follow a shape, address, complaint, petition, and often a turn toward trust. Why might it help a grieving person to have a form to follow rather than just being told to pray?
discussion.behind: Get the room to see lament as a learnable practice. We tell the suffering to pray and leave them with no idea how, and the Psalms hand them a structure. Help them feel that the form is a gift, a path through the dark, not a formula that fakes the feeling but a shape that holds the honesty.

discussion.q: Psalm 13 turns at the end, but I have trusted in your steadfast love. Is that turn the goal of every lament, or can it become a pressure to fake an ending you have not reached?
discussion.behind: This is the central tension of the session. The turn is real and good, but if we make it mandatory we teach people to perform a resolution they do not have. Hold both. The turn in Psalm 13 is genuine, and the demand that every prayer must turn is exactly the pressure that drove out honesty in session one.

discussion.q: Psalm 88 does not turn. It ends with darkness as the psalmist's only friend, and then it just stops. What does it mean to you that God kept this psalm in the Bible?
discussion.behind: Land the hardest and most freeing point of the whole study. We expect every prayer to resolve, and here is one that refuses to, preserved by God himself. The aim is permission, deep and theological, that a prayer ending in the dark is still prayer, and that the person whose night has not lifted is not praying wrong.

discussion.q: Bell admits he has tried to force the turn, to tack a hopeful ending onto a grief that had not earned one, because the dark felt like a failure. Where have you rushed yourself or someone else to the resolution?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication. Many of us cannot tolerate an unresolved grief, our own or another's, and we hurry it toward a bow. Invite honest recognition, the leader first, of how we force the turn. The point is not guilt but the freedom to let a lament stay open as long as it needs to.

objections.objection: If the lament psalms keep asking how long and accusing God of hiding his face, is not that disrespectful? You do not talk to the Almighty that way. These prayers sound like the psalmist is putting God on trial.
objections.response: Bell grants the instinct behind this, the reverence that does not want to presume on God. Then he points at the text. The psalmist does put God on trial, in a sense, and God kept the transcript. Psalm 13 asks how long four times. Psalm 88 accuses God of casting the soul into the depths. The God who inspired these prayers is evidently not threatened by the honesty in them, and a reverence that is more careful than Scripture is not reverence at all, it is fear wearing reverence as a mask. The boldness of lament is not disrespect. It is the boldness of a child who is sure enough of his father to bring him the worst of what he feels. To soften the prayers into polite requests is to lose the very thing that makes them prayers of faith, the conviction that God is real, present, and able to bear our whole heart.

objections.objection: Psalm 88 is too dark. It must be in the Bible as a negative example, the wrong way to pray, because surely God does not want us to end in despair with no hope at all.
objections.response: Treat this gently, because it is the move we all want to make, the refusal to let the dark be the dark. But look at how the psalm is framed. It is a maskil, a teaching psalm, given for instruction, attributed to the sons of Korah, set to music for corporate worship. Israel sang this. It was not preserved as a warning but as a prayer the congregation prayed together. And notice that even at its darkest it is addressed to the God of my salvation and cries out day and night before him. That is not despair that has given up. It is faith holding on by its fingernails, still talking to God when there is nothing left but the talking. The psalm does not teach us to despair. It teaches us that you can be in the dark, still clinging, still crying out, and be praying rightly. To call it a negative example is to take away the one psalm written for the person whose night has not ended.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Is there a grief in your life that has never reached its turn, where the how long is still unanswered, and have you let yourself believe that an unresolved prayer can still be a faithful one?
sessions.practice: This week, pray Psalm 13 slowly, one movement a day if you need to. Sit in the complaint before you rush to the turn. Then, on another day, pray Psalm 88, all the way to its dark final line, and do not add anything after it. Let it end where it ends. Notice what it is like to pray a prayer that does not fix anything, and write down whether being allowed to stay in the dark changed how you carried it.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you gave us the how long and you did not take it back. You kept Psalm 13 with its turn and Psalm 88 with no turn at all, and in keeping both you told us the truth, that some nights the morning comes and some nights it does not, and you are God of both. We confess we have rushed the grieving toward resolution, ourselves included, because the dark frightened us. Teach us to sit in it without lying about it. And where our own how long has gone unanswered, hold us in the asking, even when the answer does not come. God of our salvation, we cry out to you day and night. Amen.
reflection: Which is harder for me to believe, that I am allowed to complain to God as bluntly as Psalm 13 does, or that a prayer can end in the dark like Psalm 88 and still be faithful?
Where have I forced a turn toward hope onto a grief that had not arrived there, and what did that cost the honesty of my prayer?
If God kept the prayer that does not resolve in his own book, what does that say about how he meets me on the night the morning does not come?
sessions.teaching: The lament psalms have a shape, and the shape is a gift, because it hands the grieving a path to walk when they have no idea how to pray. If you read enough of them you start to see the same movements recur. There is an address, the prayer turns to face God and names him. There is a complaint, the trouble laid out plainly, sometimes against enemies, sometimes against the body, sometimes against God himself for seeming absent. There is a petition, a specific request, do something, see me, answer me. And very often there is a turn, near the end the prayer pivots toward trust, a vow of praise, a remembering of who God is. Psalm 13 is the textbook case, short enough to hold in your hand. It opens with that fourfold how long, O Lord, how long will you forget me, how long will you hide your face, how long must I bear this sorrow. It names the enemy who is winning. It asks God to consider and answer, to light up the eyes before death closes them. And then it turns. But I have trusted in your steadfast love, my heart shall rejoice in your salvation, I will sing to the Lord because he has dealt bountifully with me. The prayer that began in the dark ends in song. So the first question is what to make of that turn. The natural instinct, and a strong one, is to say the turn is the point. The lament is the runway and the praise is the takeoff. A lament is only finished when it resolves into trust, and if your prayer has not turned yet, you simply have not prayed it through. Take that instinct at full strength, because Psalm 13 really does turn, and the turn is no small thing. It is the movement of faith refusing to let the complaint be the last word. To deny that the turn matters would be to flatten the Psalms into mere catharsis. But now set Psalm 88 beside Psalm 13, and feel the floor shift. Psalm 88 has the address, it begins O Lord, God of my salvation, I cry out day and night before you. It has the complaint, an unbroken catalog of abandonment, the soul full of troubles, life drawing near to the grave, the wrath of God lying heavy, companions driven away. It has the petition, why do you hide your face, the cry going up every morning. But it does not have the turn. There is no but. There is no vow of praise, no remembering of better days, no light at the end. The last line, in the Hebrew, ends on a single word, and that word is darkness. You have caused my beloved and my friend to shun me, my companions have become darkness. And then the psalm simply stops. No resolution. No dawn. The morning does not come. And here is the verdict this entire session exists to protect. Psalm 88 is in the Bible too. God kept it. The same Spirit who preserved the turn in Psalm 13 preserved the unbroken dark of Psalm 88 and put no asterisk on it, no editorial note explaining that this is the wrong way to feel. He gave it to Israel to sing, a teaching psalm, sung in the congregation, which means the people of God were handed words for the night that does not end and told, this too is prayer. Think about what that means for the person sitting in your group whose grief has not turned. The one whose child did not recover, whose marriage did not heal, whose depression has not lifted in years of asking. We have been telling that person, with our relentlessly resolving worship, that they are stuck, that real faith would have reached the song by now, that their unending night is a sign of something wrong with them. And Psalm 88 stands up in the middle of the Bible and says no. You can cry out and not feel better. You can pray faithfully and stay in the dark. The lament that never resolves is not a failed lament. It is a faithful one, because the man in Psalm 88 is still talking to God on the last line, still calling him the God of my salvation, still crying out day and night, and that is not despair, that is faith holding on with nothing left but the grip. And I have to confess that I am the one who forces the turn. I have done it in my own prayers, tacking a hopeful ending onto a grief that had not earned one because the open wound felt like a failure of faith. I have done it to other people, hurrying them toward the silver lining because I could not bear to leave them in the dark. The God who kept Psalm 88 is more patient with our darkness than we are. So learn the shape, all of it. Let the turn come when it comes, and it will come, on many nights it truly will. But do not manufacture it. Do not lie. And when the night is one of the nights that does not turn, know that you are not praying wrong. You are praying Psalm 88, and so did the people of God, and so, we will see, did the Son of God from the cross.

scriptureStudy.note: How long, O Lord, four times in two verses. This is the address and the complaint, the prayer facing God and laying out the sorrow without softening it. The repetition is not faithlessness, it is the form, the impatience of a heart that still expects God to act.

Consider and answer me, O Lord my God, light up my eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death. This is the petition, a specific request, that God would see, answer, and revive before the darkness wins. Lament always asks for something, which is what separates it from mere despair.

But I have trusted in your steadfast love, my heart shall rejoice. This is the turn, and it is real, the pivot from complaint to trust. Note it does not deny the sorrow of the first verses, it holds the trust and the sorrow together, refusing to let the complaint be the final word.

O Lord, God of my salvation, I cry out day and night before you. The address, and notice how high it is, the God of my salvation, even as everything that follows will be dark. The relationship is intact even when the comfort is gone.

But I, O Lord, cry to you, in the morning my prayer comes before you. O Lord, why do you cast my soul away. Even here, deep in the psalm, the prayer keeps coming every morning. The why is an accusation, but it is an accusation made to God, which keeps it prayer and not abandonment.

My companions have become darkness. The final line, ending on darkness with no turn, no resolution. God kept this as the close of the psalm, which means a prayer is allowed to end in the dark, and the one praying it is not praying wrong.

O Lord, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear. The prophet uses the same how long, complaining to God about violence and injustice he does not answer. Lament is not only personal grief, it is also the protest that calls God to act on what is wrong.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the structure and theology of the lament psalms with the help of Walter Brueggemann, whose The Message of the Psalms reads the Psalter as a movement between what he called orientation, disorientation, and new orientation. The praise psalms of orientation describe a world that is reliably good, where the righteous flourish and God is plainly in charge. But life does not stay there, and the psalms of disorientation, the laments, give voice to the seasons when the reliable world has collapsed, when the innocent suffer and God seems absent. Brueggemann argued that the church, in its discomfort, tends to skip straight from orientation to a premature new orientation, leaping over the disorientation as though it could be bypassed, and that this leap is exactly what cheats the suffering of their own prayers. A serious group should consider his observation that Psalm 88 is the great refusal of the easy leap, the psalm that stays in the disorientation and will not be hurried out of it. Set this beside the older Christian reading, which sometimes treated Psalm 88 as a prophecy of Christ's own descent into the dark, his being abandoned and laid in the grave, so that the psalm of the unending night becomes, in the larger story, the psalm Jesus himself would live. Weigh the danger on both sides. The danger of leaping too fast, which silences the grieving, and the danger of romanticizing the dark, treating despair as more honest than hope, which is its own distortion. The discipline is to let the lament be a real movement, with a real shape, that may turn and may not, and to trust that the God who authored the whole Psalter is at home in every part of it, the song on the mountain and the silence at the bottom of the pit.
